t: Maximum Nesting Depth of Two Valid Parentheses Strings
o: We must color each parenthesis of a valid parentheses string with 0 or 1 so that both colors form valid parentheses strings, minimizing the maximum nesting depth of the two. Since every '(' must be matched by a later ')' of the same color, a coloring is valid iff within each color, prefixes have at least as many '(' as ')'. The key observation: the answer's optimal depth is ceil(maxDepth(seq)/2), because we can alternate the two halves of nesting levels between A and B. For example, "(()())" has max depth 2; assigning level-1 brackets to one string and level-2 brackets to the other gives depth 1 for each, matching output [0,1,1,1,1,0]. With n up to 10000, an O(n) single pass is trivially sufficient.
k: A split into two VPS's is exactly an assignment where each color never has more ')' than '(' in any prefix.
The minimum achievable max depth is ceil(d/2) where d is the original maximum nesting depth.
Assigning each bracket based on its nesting level parity (or current running depth parity) achieves this bound in one pass.

a.n: Approach 1: Greedy by Running Depth Parity (Optimal)
a.i: Track the current nesting depth while scanning. Give each bracket to string A when the depth before processing it is even, and to B when odd. Then each string only ever contains brackets from alternating depth layers, so its internal depth is about half the original — specifically max(depth(A), depth(B)) = ceil(d/2). Correctness: each color's prefix balance stays non-negative since brackets are consumed in matched pairs layer by layer.
s: For each character, record cur = depth (depth before update).
If char is '(', assign answer[i] = cur % 2 then increment depth; if ')', decrement depth first and assign answer[i] = newDepth % 2.
a.t: O(n) — single pass over the string.
a.sp: O(1) extra space besides the output array.

a.i: First compute the nesting level of every bracket (level of '(' is its depth after increment; level of ')' is its depth before decrement). Then assign bracket i to string (level[i] % 2). This is conceptually identical to Approach 1 but separates 'compute levels' from 'assign', making the ceil(d/2) bound easier to explain: levels 0..d-1 are split evenly into two groups, each reaching depth ceil(d/2).
s: Scan once computing level[i] for each index: increment depth on '(' and store old depth, or decrement on ')' and store new depth.
Also track the maximum depth d seen.
a.sp: O(n) for the auxiliary level array.

w: In an interview, present Approach 1 directly: it is one pass, O(n) time, O(1) space, and easy to prove correct via prefix-balance arguments. Common pitfalls: forgetting that ')' must use the depth *after* decrementing (so matched pairs get the same color); assuming both strings must be contiguous subsequences (they need not be); and trying to actually build A and B rather than just outputting the assignment. Edge cases: fully nested strings like "((()))" (answer alternates 0,1,0,1,0,1 giving depth 2 each vs original 3), and single pair "()" which can go entirely to one string. Follow-ups: prove the lower bound ceil(d/2) (a single string must contain some pair spanning all d levels... more precisely, by pigeonhole two adjacent levels share a color along some root-to-leaf path), or generalize to splitting into k VPS's with min max depth ceil(d/k).
